svg.title: Six steps from one laptop waking up to a campus-wide slowdown, with the reasons a topology change spreads and the mitigations that stop it
svg.desc: A vertical chain of six steps. An access port goes up when a laptop wakes. The switch reports a topology change toward the root. The root sets the topology change bit in its configuration BPDUs. Every switch shortens its MAC ageing timer. Tables empty and traffic is flooded to be relearned. Repeated per port, the whole building feels slow. Two boxes on the right explain why the signal spreads, because a topology change describes the whole topology rather than one segment, and give the mitigations: PortFast on every edge port, monitoring the topology change counter, and treating a flapping port as a design fault.
svg.text: One laptop wakes up, and for thirty-five seconds the whole building is slightly broken
Nothing in this chain is malfunctioning. Every device is doing exactly what the standard says
An access port comes up
a laptop wakes, a phone is plugged in, a PC reboots for updates
The switch reports a topology change
a port entering forwarding is a change, so a TCN is sent toward the root
The root set the change bit
its configuration BPDUs now carry the topology change flag, for thirty-five seconds
Every switch shortens its ageing timer
MAC ageing drops from five minutes to the forwarding delay, everywhere at once
Tables empty and traffic is flooded
known unicast becomes unknown unicast; every switch relearns by flooding
The users call it "the network is slow"
CPU up, brief loss, ARP honoured more slowly — and it repeats per port, per hour
WHY IT SPREADS
A topology change is a statement about the
whole topology, not about one segment.
No switch can tell which unicast entries
actually became wrong, so all of them are
treated as suspect and all of them expire.
the signal is cheap to send and expensive to receive
MITIGATION, IN ORDER OF VALUE
1. PortFast on every edge port: the change
is never generated in the first place.
2. Push it by template, not port by port,
or the one forgotten port stays loud.
3. Read the counter: topology change
count per port tells you who is flapping.
A topology change storm is a design problem, not a protocol problem. The standard is behaving; the design put hundreds of edge ports under a protocol built for trunks.
The tell is in the diagnosis: if pings are fine but everything feels slower after a floor of users arrives at nine in the morning, look at the topology change counters before you look at the uplinks.
The fix costs one template. The alternative — buying bandwidth to absorb replays — buys nothing, because the retransmissions are not a capacity problem.
